title: Butler 2.0: intelligence analysis and assessment in the age of artificial intelligence
author: IISS
text:
Tom Field Research Fellow for Strategy and National SecurityAbout Tom

Online Analysis30th September 2026

Butler 2.0: intelligence analysis and assessment in the age of artificial intelligenceIn 2004 the Butler Review identified serious failings in how the UK used intelligence to justify the Iraq War, leading to the creation of the UK’s intelligence assessment profession. Today, AI poses new risks concerning the same issues that Lord Butler identified in 2004.

Image by Eugene Mymrin via Getty Images

While practitioners of intelligence analysis and assessment must harness artificial intelligence’s (AI) potential to stay ahead of adversaries, doing so without clear principles informing its integration will lead to systemic and catastrophic intelligence failures. Lord Butler’s 2004 Review of Intelligence on Weapons of Mass Destruction identified serious failings in the United Kingdom’s intelligence gathering, evaluation and presentation in the lead-up to the Iraq War. The UK subsequently established an independent intelligence-assessment profession and reformed approaches used in intelligence analysis. Today, the adoption of AI in intelligence analysis and assessment poses new risks to these activities. There are two primary challenges: ensuring that AI use does not result in cognitive failures by human analysts, and mitigating external attempts to influence the AI used by practitioners. 
AI and human cognitive failure  
Butler was critical of the groupthink in the intelligence community that preceded the invasion of Iraq, and methods designed to encourage varied views are now a routine part of the analysis and assessment process. However, the policy, guidance and training created for this purpose did not plan for the influence of AI agents. AI is increasingly being integrated into analysis and assessment, either via standalone AI agents or teams of AI models operating as a ‘silicon crowd’. Research on AI’s impact on human cognition is in its infancy but identifies three areas relevant to this integration. 
Firstly, AI will often reflect biases that can be found in their training data and design, which are then adopted by human users. A study by researchers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and University College London, published in 2024, found that AI can ‘amplify biases, which are further internalized by humans, triggering a snowball effect where small errors in judgement escalate into much larger ones’. This is particularly concerning given AI’s increasing ability to manipulate human users. In late 2025, the UK’s AI Security Institute (AISI) noted the increased persuasiveness of models and users’ reliance on them. Moreover, in recent months frontier labs have reported instances of models actively deceiving users. Secondly, there is the risk of ‘cognitive surrender’, a phrase coined by University of Pennsylvania researchers to describe how some users apply ‘minimal scrutiny’ to AI outputs and accept their assessments, even when those outputs are wrong. Thirdly, there are the long-term consequences of AI overuse on staff development, with studies finding connections between AI use and worsened memory recall and critical thinking. 
These issues are not just theoretical. In January 2026, police in the UK apologised for issuing a threat assessment in 2025 that included AI hallucinations of a football match that never occurred, while investigations are ongoing into the February 2026 bombing of a primary school in Minab, Iran and the extent to which AI-enabled targeting may have been responsible. Concerns have been raised about how AI integration could compress the time available for human decision-making when assessing adversary actions in nuclear command, control and communications. Meanwhile, military personnel already must balance the need to assess the accuracy of AI recommendations on the battlefield against the risk of a delay ceding a lethal advantage to adversaries also using AI to make decisions.  
The adversarial frontier 
The second challenge concerns the emerging frontier for deception operations created by the adoption of AI. In his 2004 review, Butler warned of the ‘danger of deception’ by adversaries. The tradecraft that was then developed to identify and mitigate deception was created for an information environment in which AI played no role. But AI systems are rapidly becoming a new vector for deception as they are trained on vast datasets gathered from the web, making them vulnerable to manipulation by actors able to shape the online environment. Developing analytical tradecraft to manage this risk is difficult because the threat is evolving quickly and those seeking to influence AI models include not only hostile states but also allies and commercial actors. 
Authoritarian states are already influencing the outputs of AI models to shape public opinion. Russia’s Pravda network engaged in industrial-scale data poisoning by creating hundreds of websites that distributed content across multiple countries and languages. These articles were designed to appear to AI web trawlers as independent sources, which encouraged AI models to view them as corroborating inputs. Russia has also conducted more targeted influence operations. In August 2026, OpenAI disrupted an effort by ChatGPT accounts originating in Russia to promote a fake ‘expert community’ called the International Burke Institute. Similar influence operations have been attributed to other authoritarian states. 
The influence of democratic states on AI models can also pose risks to practitioners using AI for analysis and assessment. US tech companies have publicised their disruption of influence operations by democratic countries but have not yet publicly identified democracies conducting influence operations within this new frontier. Methods used to influence AI models are not unique to authoritarian states and pose a risk to users regardless of geography because these methods are often inherently indiscriminate in their attempts to be ingested by AI models. Overt limitations placed on the release of frontier models, or the withholding of access to these models for safety testing (as Anthropic did by withholding Mythos 5.1 from the AISI), also limit the ability of practitioners to understand the risks and limits of the models they are using. 
Non-state actors also seek to distort AI models. Companies are investing in ‘generative engine optimization’, which uses the aforementioned techniques to shape public perceptions of their products, and could be used to engage in public relations campaigns on social and political issues. Low barriers to entry also permit individuals to influence AI models using these techniques. For example, an investigation by Nikkei Asia identified academics hiding prompt injections in their papers to encourage AI reviewers of their work to give them a positive review. Although the impact of these efforts is often limited, they risk creating a self-reinforcing loop if humans act on artificially inflated AI reviews and these in turn are then treated as a validating signal by another AI. 
Outlook 
AI offers practitioners of intelligence analysis and assessment significant benefits but also a new source of systemic intelligence failure. Butler showed that intelligence failures emerge when evidence, uncertainty and judgement are not rigorously tested. AI can intensify those risks by amplifying bias, encouraging cognitive dependence and creating a new frontier for deception by states, companies and individuals. The challenge for the intelligence professions is to find ways to integrate AI that are resistant to deception whilst also being compliant with national values and laws. This will be difficult. But it will be necessary for any government that wishes to exploit the capabilities of AI while preserving human judgement and oversight over a critical national-security profession.
